name: House of Terror (Terror Háza)
funding: Mária Schmidt's public foundation ran it from 2002 to 2026 on government money, 5.5 billion forints in 2019. Since September 2026 a culture ministry company, Kulturális Vagyonkezelő Kft, runs it.
watch: At Andrássy út 60, once Arrow Cross and ÁVH headquarters. Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr dismissed Schmidt on 15 September 2026 and ordered a content review.

propaganda.summary: The first Orbán government opened it on 24 February 2002 under Orbán's adviser Mária Schmidt; historians criticised its equation of fascism and communism and its casting of Hungary as a victim of foreign occupiers.

name: Akureyri Art Museum (Listasafnið á Akureyri)
funding: Run by the town of Akureyri under a state cultural agreement: for 2021 to 2023 the state gave ISK 230M a year for the town's institutions, the museum among them, matched by the town.
watch: Just south of the Arctic Circle, at about 65.7°N; it has hosted the Icelandic Visual Arts Awards since 2006.
records_note: Publishes its programme and opening hours; the museum's own budget line was not found.

name: Museum of PKI Treachery
funding: In the state Pancasila Sakti complex at Lubang Buaya, jointly managed by the Indonesian military (TNI) and the Education and Culture Ministry. Admission is 5,000 rupiah.
watch: Opened by President Suharto on 1 October 1992 with 34 dioramas; tens of thousands of visitors a year, mostly schools. A wing opened in 2013.

propaganda.summary: Suharto's Army History Centre opened the museum in 1992; its 34 dioramas present the New Order account of PKI treachery in 1965 and omit the mass killings that followed.

name: National Museum of the Islamic Revolution and Holy Defense
funding: Tehran municipality built it, and its statute makes the municipality responsible for the budget and staff.
watch: Opened in 2012 in Tehran's Abbas-Abad district; about 300,000 visitors a year (AFP, 2018). The Armed Forces General Staff published its statute amendments in 2021.

propaganda.summary: The Tehran municipality built it. Its statute was amended in 2021 with Supreme Leader Khamenei's approval and published by the Armed Forces General Staff. AFP reported that it glorifies the Iran-Iraq war.

name: Palazzo delle Esposizioni
funding: Owned by Roma Capitale and run under a city service contract by Azienda Speciale Palaexpo, a 1998 municipal body that also runs the Scuderie del Quirinale and Casa del Jazz.
watch: Opened 1883 on Via Nazionale to a design by Pio Piacentini; reopened in 2007 after restoration.

propaganda.summary: The National Fascist Party under Dino Alfieri staged the Mostra della Rivoluzione Fascista here from 28 October 1932, opened by Mussolini, behind a fasces facade by Libera and De Renzi; nearly four million people attended.

name: Quadriennale di Roma
funding: Fondazione La Quadriennale di Roma is funded by its partners: the Ministry of Culture, Roma Capitale's Department of Culture, the Lazio Region and the Rome Chamber of Commerce.
watch: Founded by Rome's Governorate in 1927, first held in 1931 at the Palazzo delle Esposizioni, an autonomous body since 1937; based at Villa Carpegna.

propaganda.summary: Under Cipriano Efisio Oppo the 1931 to 1943 Quadriennali built consensus for the fascist regime; the 1935 halls celebrated regime policies and Mussolini, and the 1939 edition ran under ministerial supervision and racial laws.

name: Yūshūkan
funding: Maintained by Yasukuni Shrine, a private religious corporation since 1946, when the Occupation's Shinto Directive ended state sponsorship of Shinto. The revamped museum reopened in July 1986.
watch: Japan's first Western-style museum, opened February 1882 on the shrine grounds; scholars criticise its revisionist account that omits the experiences of China and Korea.

propaganda.summary: Established in 1882 under the Imperial Army and made a state institution of the Army Ministry by imperial decree in 1910, it ran national spiritual mobilisation exhibitions in the 1930s until September 1945.

name: Kaysone Phomvihane Museum
funding: Built with non-refundable Vietnamese aid on a 1992 Politburo decision and opened in December 2000; in 2014 Vietnam funded a 14 billion dong refurbishment. The Lao state runs it.
watch: A bronze statue of Kaysone stands outside; the Party's Propaganda and Training Board stages its anniversary exhibitions, opened by General Secretary Thongloun Sisoulith in 2025.

propaganda.summary: The Party Politburo decided in 1992 to build a museum to the Party's founder; Vietnam funded it and it opened in 2000. The Party's Propaganda and Training Board holds its anniversary exhibitions.

name: Defence Services Museum
funding: Run by the Tatmadaw, Myanmar's armed forces: the museum and its Historical Research Institute sit under the Commander-in-Chief's office. Soldiers control its gates and active-duty units supply its docents.
watch: The 603 acre site in Zeyathiri Township has twelve display halls of about 540,000 square feet; civilian visitors are rare and staff often outnumber them.

propaganda.summary: The military government opened the 603 acre museum in March 2012. Run by the Tatmadaw, it presents the armed forces' nationalist ideology, with portraits of Ne Win, Than Shwe and Min Aung Hlaing throughout.

name: Drug Elimination Museum
funding: Created by the Ministry of Home Affairs under Than Shwe's State Peace and Development Council; the ministry still pays a skeleton staff and a police major runs it.
watch: Three floors of exhibits on a 15.11 acre former cemetery; visitors are mostly students on free field trips, and others pay 4,000 kyat.

propaganda.summary: Than Shwe's junta inaugurated the museum on 26 June 2001 to publicise its drug eradication campaign. Exhibits cast drugs as a foreign enemy and quote a general calling human rights and democracy big-nation excuses.
